issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in convicting the appellant under section 419 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code when no charge for this offence was framed in the trial court, and the appellant was not questioned about it under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: The appellant was convicted by a trial court for several offenses, including conspiracy, cheating, and forgery.

On appeal, the High Court did not rule on the original charges. Instead, it convicted the appellant for a new offense: abetting cheating by personation under section 419 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code.
The basis for the High Court's new conviction was its finding that the appellant had deceived an Oath Commissioner by wrongly identifying a person who was signing a false affidavit.
law: For a conviction to be valid, the accused must be formally charged with the specific offense in the trial court.
The accused must be questioned about the evidence relating to the charge under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to give them an opportunity to explain.

For an act to constitute the offense of "cheating," the deception must induce the person deceived to do something that causes, or is likely to cause, damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation, or property.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court made two critical errors.

First, there was a procedural error: the appellant was never charged with the offense of cheating the Oath Commissioner, nor was he questioned about it during the trial. This violated the principles of a fair trial.

Second, there was a substantive legal error: the facts did not constitute the offense of cheating the Oath Commissioner. The Court reasoned that while the Commissioner was deceived into attesting the affidavit, this act did not cause, nor was it likely to cause, any damage or harm to him in body, mind, reputation, or property. Since this essential ingredient of cheating was missing, the conviction was legally unsustainable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred both procedurally and substantively. It set aside the conviction under section 419/109 IPC because no charge was framed, the appellant was not questioned on it, and the facts did not legally constitute the offense of cheating. The case was sent back to the High Court for a decision on the original charges.

issue.issue_text: Whether the facts found, specifically inducing an Oath Commissioner to attest an affidavit by wrong identification, constituted the offence of cheating.

facts: The appellant was found to have deceived an Oath Commissioner by wrongly identifying a person.
This deception induced the Oath Commissioner to attest an affidavit, believing it was sworn by the person being identified (Govind Ram).
law: The Court analyzed the definition of "cheating" under Section 415 of the Indian Penal Code.

To constitute cheating, the person deceived must be induced to do an act they would not otherwise do, and that act must cause or be likely to cause "damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property."
Alternatively, the person must be dishonestly induced to deliver property, which was not the case here.
application: The Court applied the legal definition of cheating to the specific facts concerning the Oath Commissioner.

It determined that while the Oath Commissioner was deceived and induced to act (attest the affidavit), this act of attestation could not possibly cause any damage or harm to the Oath Commissioner himself in his body, mind, reputation, or property.
Since one of the essential ingredients of the offence—the likelihood of damage or harm to the person deceived—was not established, the definition of cheating was not met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the facts did not constitute the offence of cheating because the act of attesting the affidavit, while induced by deception, was not likely to cause any damage or harm to the Oath Commissioner, which is a necessary element of the offence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court failed in its duty by not recording a clear finding on the offences for which the appellant was convicted by the trial court.

facts: The appellant was convicted by a trial court for several offences.
On appeal, the High Court did not examine the evidence or record any findings on the facts related to the offences for which the trial court had convicted the appellant.
law: An appellate court, when hearing an appeal against a conviction, has a duty to examine the evidence and record clear findings on the offences for which the appellant was convicted by the lower court.
application: The Supreme Court observed that the High Court, by convicting the appellant for a new offence with which he was never charged, had adopted an "extraordinary course."

The Supreme Court explicitly stated that in doing so, the High Court "failed to record a clear finding whether the offences, for which the appellant had been convicted by the trial Court, were proved or not."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, finding that the High Court had failed in its duty. It set aside the High Court's conviction and remitted the case back to the High Court for a rehearing, with instructions to decide the appeal in respect of the specific offences for which the appellant was convicted by the trial court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction for an offense cannot be sustained when no charge was framed for it and the accused was not questioned on the evidence relating to that specific charge. Furthermore, the offense of cheating is not constituted if the deceived person was not induced to deliver any property, consent to the retention of any property, or perform an act likely to cause damage or harm to their body, mind, reputation, or property.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's conviction of the appellant for abetting cheating was set aside because it was procedurally flawed, substantively incorrect, and represented a failure of appellate duty. The appellant was never charged with this new offence nor questioned about the related evidence under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Furthermore, the act of wrongly identifying a person to an Oath Commissioner does not legally constitute cheating, as the Oath Commissioner was not induced to deliver or consent to the retention of any property. Finally, in substituting the conviction, the High Court failed in its duty to record a clear finding on the original offences for which the appellant was convicted by the trial court, necessitating a remand for rehearing.
legal_tests_applied: The elements of the offence of 'cheating' as defined in the Indian Penal Code, specifically that the act of deception must induce the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property.

The procedural requirement under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that an accused must be questioned on and given an opportunity to explain the evidence relating to the specific charge for which they are being tried.
policy_considerations: Convicting an accused for an offence for which no charge was framed and about which they were not questioned during their examination is a violation of the principles of natural justice, as the accused is not given a fair opportunity to defend themselves against that specific accusation.
An appellate court, when altering or substituting a conviction from a trial court, has a duty to record a clear finding as to whether the original offences were proven or not.
